observation.visible_scene: Nighttime view of a large, wide waterfall (Niagara Falls) illuminated with blue lights. A massive cloud of mist/steam rises from the crest of the falls and fills the upper-center of the frame against a dark, partly clouded sky. In the foreground is a dark, choppy water surface, a metal railing at lower-left, and a rock at lower-center. Distant warm city lights line the left horizon and a string of white lights (a bridge) crosses the right horizon. A single bright point light is visible through the mist near the middle-left of the plume.
visible_changes: The mist plume above the falls continuously billows and deforms: its top edge and side contours change shape from frame to frame, and the column appears to lean/drift slightly as it rises, rather than translating as a rigid object.
The foreground water surface shows shifting ripples and wave crests (turbulent, ongoing motion), changing pattern between frames.
The blue illumination on the falling-water curtain and on the lower mist stays steady and persistent throughout the excerpt; the lit waterfall edge does not move.

There is a small, slow handheld drift of the camera: the railing, the foreground rock, the left city lights, and the right bridge lights shift slightly relative to the frame edges over the clip, indicating minor camera motion rather than object motion.
The bright point light seen through the mist keeps roughly the same position within the plume, consistent with a fixed light source whose apparent location moves only with the slight camera drift.
outside_clip_unknowns: The wind strength/direction that drives the mist billowing is not directly visible.
Whether the plume ultimately grows, dissipates, or shifts after t=1.334 s is outside the excerpt.
The full height and far edges of the falls and the source of the blue lighting are not shown.
uncertain_details: The exact direction and magnitude of the camera drift are small and ambiguous; it is handheld jitter rather than a clear pan or zoom.
Whether the mist column leans net left or net right over the segment is hard to confirm given its constant internal deformation.
The single bright dot is interpreted as a fixed light seen through mist, but its identity cannot be confirmed from the frames.
